blocks.text: The results of mechanical tests are usually expressed in terms of stress and strain, which are defined in terms of applied force and deformation.

blocks.title: Stress
blocks.text: Stress is the force applied per unit area to produce any change in the shape, volume or length of a body: stress (sigma) = force (F) / area (A) ... (5.1). The SI unit of stress is the newton per square metre (N m^-2), given the name pascal (Pa). When a stress changes length it is called tensile stress, when it changes volume it is volume stress, and when it changes shape it is shear stress.

blocks.title: Strain
blocks.text: Strain is a measure of the deformation of a solid when stress is applied to it. For deformation in one dimension, strain is the fractional change in length: if delta L is the change in length and L the original length (Fig. 5.3a), strain (epsilon) = change in length (delta L) / original length (L) ... (5.2). Being a ratio of lengths, strain is dimensionless and has no units. Strain due to tensile stress is tensile strain, and strain produced by compressive stress is compressive strain.

blocks.alt: A pink bar of length L is pulled by a force F at each end, the arrows pointing outward. Dotted outlines beyond both ends show how far the bar is stretched.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.3(a): Tensile strain (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.3(a)).

blocks.title: Volumetric strain
blocks.text: When the applied stress changes the volume, the change in volume per unit volume is the volumetric strain (Fig. 5.3b): volumetric strain = delta V / V ... (5.3).

blocks.alt: A cube drawn in outline with a smaller dashed cube inside it. Red arrows labelled F press inward on every face: from the top, the bottom, the left, the right, the front and the back. Wavy leaders label a face A, the outer cube Volume V and the inner dashed cube Volume V - delta V.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.3(b): Volumetric strain (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.3(b)).

blocks.title: Shear strain
blocks.text: If y is the distance between two opposite faces of a rigid body subjected to shear stress and one face slides through delta x (Fig. 5.3c), the shear strain is gamma = delta x / y = tan theta ... (5.4); for small theta measured in radians tan theta is about theta, so gamma = theta ... (5.5).

blocks.alt: A grey block, its base fixed, leans to the right. A force F acts to the right along its orange top face, labelled A. A vertical line of height y rises from the fixed bottom corner; the top edge has slid a distance delta x beyond it, and the angle theta is marked between the vertical line and the slanted side.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.3(c): Shear strain (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.3(c)).

blocks.title: Young's modulus
blocks.text: The stress applied per unit strain is called Young's modulus: Y = tensile stress / tensile strain = (F/A) / (delta L / L) ... (5.6). It has the same unit as stress, N m^-2 or Pa. Although named after the 19th-century British scientist Thomas Young, the concept was developed in 1727 by Leonhard Euler (For Your Information). There are various methods to determine the Young's modulus of a wire; one is Searle's method.
